blocks.text: Imagine a board game where each player's move depends only on their current position, not how they got there. This is the essence of a Markov Chain.

blocks.markdown: Markov Chains are mathematical systems that undergo transitions from one state to another on a state space. They are memoryless, meaning the next state depends only on the current state and not on the sequence of events that preceded it.

blocks.title: Markov Chain
blocks.text: A Markov Chain is a stochastic process that satisfies the Markov property: the probability of moving to the next state depends only on the present state and not on the previous states.

blocks.markdown: To formalize this, we use a **transition matrix**, which is a square matrix used to describe the transitions of a Markov Chain. Each element $P_{ij}$ of the matrix represents the probability of transitioning from state $i$ to state $j$.

blocks.latex: P = \begin{bmatrix} P_{11} & P_{12} & \cdots & P_{1n} \\ P_{21} & P_{22} & \cdots & P_{2n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ P_{n1} & P_{n2} & \cdots & P_{nn} \end{bmatrix}
blocks.caption: Transition Matrix of a Markov Chain

blocks.title: Constructing a Transition Matrix
blocks.prompt: Consider a simple weather model with states: Sunny (S), Cloudy (C), and Rainy (R). The transition probabilities are: Sunny to Cloudy 0.3, Sunny to Rainy 0.2, Cloudy to Sunny 0.4, Cloudy to Rainy 0.3, Rainy to Sunny 0.2, Rainy to Cloudy 0.3. Construct the transition matrix.

steps.text: Identify the states and arrange them in a consistent order: Sunny (S), Cloudy (C), Rainy (R).
Fill in the transition probabilities based on the given data.
Ensure each row sums to 1, as they represent probability distributions.

blocks.markdown: Once the transition matrix is constructed, we can compute the state distribution after $n$ steps. This is done by multiplying the initial state vector by the transition matrix $n$ times.

blocks.title: Computing State Distribution
blocks.prompt: Given the initial state vector $\mathbf{v}^{(0)} = [1, 0, 0]$, representing a sunny start, compute the state distribution after 2 steps using the transition matrix from the previous example.

steps.text: Calculate $P^2$ by multiplying the transition matrix by itself.
Multiply the initial state vector $\mathbf{v}^{(0)}$ by $P^2$ to find $\mathbf{v}^{(2)}$.

blocks.answer: After 2 steps, the state distribution is $\mathbf{v}^{(2)} = [0.41, 0.33, 0.26]$.

blocks.markdown: A **stationary distribution** is a probability distribution that remains unchanged as the system evolves. For a Markov Chain, it is a vector $\pi$ such that $\pi P = \pi$.

blocks.title: Stationary Distribution
blocks.text: The stationary distribution provides insight into the long-term behavior of a Markov Chain, indicating the proportion of time the system spends in each state.

points: Markov Chains are defined by their transition matrices, which describe the probabilities of moving between states.
State distributions after $n$ steps can be computed using matrix multiplication.
Stationary distributions reveal the long-term behavior of Markov Chains.
